TO: Rob Castellano, Chief Executive Officer; Rachel Steinberg, General Counsel
FROM: Owen Park, Chief Financial Officer

SUBJECT: Litigation Reserve Recommendation — ApexHip Product Liability (Q2 2023)

Rob, Rachel:

Following our preliminary review of Q1 close figures and in light of external developments over the past six weeks, Finance recommends an immediate adjustment to the product liability reserve established for ApexHip. Specifically, we recommend increasing the existing $18.0M accrual established in Q3 2022 by $8.0M, bringing the total litigation reserve to $26.0M effective for the Q2 2023 financial statements.

Basis for Reserve Adjustment

As discussed with Whitfield & Barr last month, the service of the initial state-court complaints in late March represents a formal transition from an unasserted potential liability to active litigation. The underlying clinical exposure cited in these initial filings tracks precisely with the registry data we reviewed internally throughout 2021:

1. NJR 7.1% 5-Year Revision Rate: The initial complaints heavily quote the March 2021 NJR annual report benchmark (7.1% vs. 3.2% class average) as prima facie evidence of elevated failure.
2. AJRR Corroboration: Late-2021 AJRR registry metrics, which demonstrated parallel divergence in domestic revision curves, have now been incorporated into plaintiff filings regarding ARMD and elevated cobalt/chromium ion levels.

Given the rate of initial filings and discussions with outside counsel regarding potential consolidation scenarios, Hannah Berg and I modeled defense costs, potential initial settlement valuations, and retention liabilities under our Aegis Specialty policy. As you know, Aegis issued a reservation of rights last year, meaning defense expense erosion will fall heavily within our direct retention before excess coverage responds. An accrual of $26.0M aligns more closely with probable and reasonably estimable losses under ASC 450.

Commercial Impact & Top-Line Drag

The legal exposure continues to compound top-line erosion. The commercial fallout from the registry disclosures, the October 2021 surgeon notification, and the residual confusion from the unrelated 2022 cup coating recall has severely impaired Apex reorder rates.

Hannah’s FP&A team has completed the updated spring forecast. ApexHip annualized revenue for FY2023 has been revised downward again, dropping from our prior budget projection of $54M to approximately $42.0M annualized. This represents a significant contraction from peak 2020 revenue ($96M) and will create an operational margin drag of roughly 180 bps across Reconstructive.

Please let me know when we can take 15 minutes to align before I brief the Audit Committee ahead of the May board meeting.

VERIDIAN ORTHOPEDICS, INC.
Post-Market Surveillance — Interim Report

Report No.: PMS-2021-014
Date: June 28, 2021
Prepared by: Greg Novak, Director, Post-Market Surveillance
Product: ApexHip Total Hip System (all cup/head/stem configurations)
Distribution: Quality, Regulatory Affairs, R&D, Clinical Affairs (internal working file, pre-decision)

1. Purpose

This interim report summarizes post-market complaint trending for ApexHip metal-ion/wear-related events alongside external registry data from the UK National Joint Registry (NJR) and preliminary American Joint Replacement Registry (AJRR) figures, for the purpose of informing a cross-functional decision on next steps.

2. Complaint Trend Summary

TrackWise complaint records coded to metal-ion elevation, ARMD, pseudotumor, or related revision-for-wear categories show a sustained upward trend since 2019. Year-over-year, complaint volume in this category is up approximately 85% (2020 vs. 2019 baseline, annualized through Q1 2021 continuing the trajectory). This is not simply a function of increased implant volume — normalized against units sold, the rate per 1,000 implants is also climbing, not flat. I want to be careful here: TrackWise coding practices shifted somewhat in 2020 (see Raman's Q4 2020 coding audit), which may account for some of the apparent increase, but even a conservative adjustment leaves a real upward signal.

3. Registry Correlation

The March 2021 NJR annual report placed ApexHip's 5-year revision rate at 7.1%, against a class average (all MoM and non-MoM large-head hip systems combined) of 3.2%. That's more than double the comparator. I've cross-tabbed the NJR cohort dates against our own launch and complaint timeline and the divergence starts becoming visible in registry data roughly 3 years post-launch, which lines up reasonably well with when we'd expect edge-loading wear effects to manifest clinically if Halvorsen's 2019 high-inclination wear-test findings are operative in the field (see his Feb 2019 memo to Raman/Mendes re: 55° inclination testing, 4-6x wear vs. the 45°-only protocol used for original clearance).

AJRR data is still preliminary — we only have partial 2021 reporting — but the early read shows a similar directional trend for large-head MoM configurations generally, ApexHip included. I'd treat the AJRR numbers as corroborating rather than conclusive at this stage; sample size and reporting lag are real limitations. I'll have a fuller AJRR cut in the Q3 update.

4. Assessment

Taken together, I think we have three independent signals now pointing the same direction: internal complaint trending, NJR, and preliminary AJRR. Individually each has caveats (coding changes, single-registry limitations, immature data), but the consistency across three sources is, in my view, more than coincidental.

I'll also flag that ECO-2019-118 — the design change proposed by Halvorsen's team following the 2019 re-testing, and deferred at the time — has not been revisited since. Given the registry correlation above, I think it's reasonable to put that decision back on the table rather than treat it as closed.

5. Recommendation

I recommend the cross-functional group (Regulatory, Quality, Clinical, R&D, and Marketing) convene formally in Q3 to review this data package in full and determine whether labeling changes, a surgeon communication, or a design/manufacturing action is warranted. Given the trajectory of both the complaint data and the registry signal, I don't think this should wait until year-end review. I'm happy to present the full data set — I can also pull a more granular breakdown by cup inclination angle from surgeon-reported operative notes if that would help inform the discussion, though that will take a couple weeks to compile.

Attachments: NJR_2021_Apex_extract.xlsx, TrackWise_MoM_trend_2019-2021.xlsx

— Greg Novak
Director, Post-Market Surveillance

ENGINEERING MEMORANDUM

Date: March 22, 2021
From: Tom Halvorsen, Sr. Design Engineer
To: KneeFlex Design History File
Subject: KneeFlex Design Change ECO-2021-044 Summary

ECO-2021-044 proposes a process change to the porous coating application used on the KneeFlex tibial baseplate. This is a manufacturing-yield change. It does not alter the finished device’s intended use, material specification, implant geometry, packaging configuration, sterilization method, or performance requirements.

1. Background and rationale

Since January, Warsaw manufacturing has seen variable yield in the tibial baseplate coating cell, primarily driven by rejects at visual inspection for incomplete coverage at the posterior edge and inconsistent surface appearance in the medial corner. The current process uses a fixed fixture angle and a single-pass application sequence. Review of batch records and line observations indicates that part orientation during the final portion of the pass is contributing to uneven deposition.

ECO-2021-044 changes the fixture orientation by 12 degrees and replaces the current single-pass sequence with two controlled passes. The proposed settings are intended to improve coverage consistency and reduce rework and scrap without changing the released coating specification. The acceptance criteria remain those currently defined in KF-WI-217 and the KneeFlex tibial baseplate drawing package.

This is not a response to a field complaint trend. There is no identified clinical or product-performance issue associated with the current process. The action is being taken to improve manufacturing yield and reduce avoidable inspection rejects.

2. Proposed verification plan

Engineering will build three pilot lots using the revised fixture and application sequence. The pilot lots will be compared against three recent production lots manufactured using the current process. Testing will include:

- Coating thickness measurements at the standard mapped locations, including posterior and medial-edge locations;
- Visual coverage inspection per KF-WI-217;
- Adhesion testing on representative coupons and baseplate samples;
- Surface roughness verification;
- Dimensional inspection of the finished baseplate after coating; and
- Review of process capability for coating thickness and visual-inspection reject rate.

The verification protocol will define sample quantities before execution. Any result outside the currently released acceptance criteria will stop implementation pending Design Assurance review. Manufacturing Engineering will also confirm that the revised fixture can be cleaned and maintained under existing work instructions.

No new clinical evaluation is proposed because the device design and coating requirements are unchanged. Regulatory Affairs will assess the completed verification package and document the basis for determining whether a new submission is required. Current assessment is that this is a manufacturing-process change within the established design envelope.

3. DHF and controlled-document updates

Before release, the following records need to be completed or revised:

- ECO-2021-044 approval record and implementation checklist;
- Updated process FMEA identifying the revised orientation and two-pass sequence;
- Revised manufacturing work instruction and fixture setup sheet;
- Verification protocol and report;
- Training records for coating-cell operators and inspectors;
- Updated process validation summary, if required by the pilot data; and
- DHF index entry linking the ECO, risk assessment, test report, and released work instructions.

The change control package should make clear that yield improvement is the reason for the change and should not characterize current production material as nonconforming unless it failed existing release criteria.

For process consistency, the change-control package follows the same template used for prior ApexHip ECOs; that reference is to document format only and does not reflect any ApexHip technical evaluation or shared design issue.

I will circulate the draft verification protocol by Friday. Manufacturing needs to reserve the coating cell for the pilot run before the April preventive-maintenance window.

Tom

Subject: RE: Active Life refresh: revision-rate slide language

Anika, Carlos,

I cannot provide medical sign-off on that statement as currently drafted.

From a regulatory and clinical standpoint, we cannot substantiate "comparable to industry leaders." The March 2021 NJR annual report puts ApexHip's 5-year cumulative revision rate at 7.1%, compared to the 3.2% class average for total hip systems in similar cohorts. Attempting to defend a comparative equivalence claim against industry benchmarks with that registry data on the public record creates a severe substantiation risk if challenged by competitors or the FDA.

I strongly recommend softening this to a strictly non-comparative formulation. Something focusing on design intent, such as: "Engineered for endurance: designed with high-congruency MoM articulation and the KinetiCoat porous surface to support stability and active lifestyles."

Let us strip out any specific comparative revision-rate claims from this promotional material until we complete our deeper internal review of the registry signals.

Best regards,

Leon

Recorded By: Priya Raman (Director, Quality & Complaint Handling)

Attendees:
- Priya Raman (Director, Quality & Complaint Handling)
- Dana Okonkwo (VP, Regulatory Affairs)
- Tom Halvorsen (Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip)
- Greg Novak (Director, Post-Market Surveillance)

1. Post-Market Complaint Summary (P. Raman)
- Quality reviewed the current complaint dataset logged under product code ApexHip (acetabular cup and femoral head/stem constructs).
- A cumulative total of 16 metal-ion related complaints have been entered into TrackWise since the initial cluster surfaced in August 2018 (starting with the Atlanta cases). Primary symptomology across these records includes unexplained groin pain, joint effusion, elevated serum Co/Cr levels (>7 ppb threshold), and preliminary indications of ARMD/local soft tissue reactions.
- P. Raman noted that while current complaint rates remain within broad internal threshold monitoring limits on a per-unit-shipped basis, the specific ARMD/metallosis signal shows an upward vector month-over-month.

2. Biomechanical Wear Simulation Findings (T. Halvorsen)
- T. Halvorsen presented data from his re-run of wear simulation protocols evaluating ApexHip assemblies at a 55° cup inclination angle (as opposed to standard nominal 45° alignment specified in ISO 14242 testing per the original DHF).
- Summary of findings: Testing at 55° inclination revealed micro-separation, edge-loading, and a 4× to 6× volumetric wear increase compared to baseline 45° simulation benchmarks.
- Halvorsen noted that surgeon cup placement in vivo frequently approaches or exceeds 50°–55° in routine patient anatomies, which could explain the accelerated ion release reported in the field.

3. Registry & Signal Surveillance (G. Novak)
- G. Novak provided an update on surveillance monitoring. While formal published annual registry cuts are not yet mature, preliminary AJRR hospital procedural data hints at early revision reporting for ApexHip tracking noticeably above the general category average for metal-on-poly and alternative bearing cohorts.
- Sample size remains small, but the revision trend is consistent with the track of complaints discussed.

4. Discussion & Disposition
- The group discussed immediate product actions. No consensus or decision was reached regarding halting sales or initiating field actions at this time; broader commercial and clinical leadership input would be required. The team agreed to focus on data capture, regulatory compliance, and potential engineering remediation.

Action Items
1. P. Raman: Update the TrackWise complaint intake form for total hip arthroplasty to include a dedicated, mandatory field capturing radiographic acetabular cup inclination angle where post-op films or surgical notes are obtainable. *(Target: Oct 18, 2019)*
2. D. Okonkwo: Evaluate MDR reportability obligations under 21 CFR 803 concerning aggregate complaint volume and recent trending patterns. *(Target: Oct 25, 2019)*

Leon, Dana,

For what it's worth, I pulled the late-2021 AJRR extract yesterday. Sample size is much smaller than NJR (fewer years of Apex volume in the US registry, obviously), but the directional trend is consistent — elevated revision rate relative to class average, same general magnitude of gap. Not enough on its own to move the needle, but it doesn't contradict NJR either.

Given that, I'm going to build out a quarterly dashboard so we're not waiting on annual publication cycles to see where we stand — NJR and AJRR extracts side by side against class average, updated every quarter. I'll set a recurring calendar reminder for the pulls so it doesn't slip.

Greg

-----Original Message-----
From: Dr. Leon Adeyemi
To: Dana Okonkwo; Greg Novak
Date: Tue, 16 Sep 2021 09:41
Subject: Follow-up thoughts on the registry data

Dana, Greg,

Wanted to put some additional thoughts down after Tuesday's meeting, mostly for my own clarity but also so we're aligned going forward.

The 7.1% five-year revision rate in the NJR report is genuinely concerning to me as a clinician, and I don't want that to get lost in how we're framing this internally. That said, I think we need to hold two possibilities open at once. The literature on edge-loading at high inclination angles is fairly consistent with what Tom's 2019 wear-test work showed at 55 degrees — and that pattern is often surgical-technique dependent rather than a pure implant design failure. Cup positioning variability across surgeons could be doing real work here, and that's not something a labeling change alone fixes, but it does mean I'm not ready to call this a design defect on the current data.

Given that, I support moving quickly on the labeling update — the sooner surgeons are reminded about inclination targets, the better. I'd also like us to pull PMS data again in six months rather than waiting for the next annual cycle.

I'm comfortable with continuing to sell under these conditions for now. But if the AJRR Q1 2022 numbers move in the wrong direction, I think we need to revisit this decision seriously.

Leon

EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE / POST-MARKET SURVEILLANCE REVIEW

MEETING MINUTES: REGISTRY SIGNAL REVIEW (APEXHIP)

Date: September 14, 2021
Time: 10:00 AM – 11:45 AM EST
Location: Executive Boardroom (Warsaw HQ) / Microsoft Teams Video Conference
Recording Secretary: Devon Mitchell (Sr. Regulatory Specialist)

ATTENDEES
* Rob Castellano, Chief Executive Officer
* Dana Okonkwo, VP Regulatory Affairs
* Dr. Leon Adeyemi, Chief Medical Officer
* Priya Raman, Director, Quality & Complaint Handling
* Greg Novak, Director, Post-Market Surveillance
* Marcus Lee, VP Sales, Reconstructive
* Carlos Mendes, Product Manager, ApexHip
* Devon Mitchell, Sr. Regulatory Specialist (Minutes)

1. CALL TO ORDER & PURPOSE
The meeting was convened at 10:02 AM by D. Okonkwo to evaluate cumulative post-market surveillance data regarding the ApexHip Total Hip System, specifically focusing on comparative registry performance trends identified in the United Kingdom National Joint Registry (NJR) 2021 Annual Report and preliminary datasets from the American Joint Replacement Registry (AJRR).

2. PRESENTATION OF REGISTRY DATA (G. NOVAK)
G. Novak presented an analysis of international and domestic joint registries through Q2 2021:
* NJR Data (UK): The ApexHip system demonstrates an estimated cumulative revision rate of 7.1% at five years post-implantation across all sizes. By comparison, the broader metal-on-metal (MoM) and hybrid total hip arthroplasty class benchmarks at an average 3.2% revision rate at the same interval.
* AJRR Data (US): US registry signal indicators parallel the NJR trend, showing an upward trajectory in revision risk specifically associated with larger diameter femoral head constructs (≥44 mm) and higher acetabular component abduction/inclination angles (>45°).
* Observed Failure Modes: The primary indications cited for revision within the registry cohorts include pain of unexplained origin, adverse reaction to metal debris (ARMD) / pseudotumor formation, and aseptic loosening.

3. CLINICAL RISK-BENEFIT ASSESSMENT (DR. L. ADEYEMI)
Dr. L. Adeyemi provided clinical context regarding the registry findings:
* The observed delta in revision rates is clinically relevant; however, the clinical benefit of high-demand stability, low dislocation rates, and reduced mechanical wear in younger, highly active patient populations remains viable when the implant is positioned strictly within the target Lewinnek safe zone (inclination ≤45°).
* The primary driver of accelerated metal-ion release and secondary local tissue reactions appears clinically correlated with surgical placement techniques (edge-loading at steep inclination angles) rather than an intrinsic systemic design flaw across all patient demographics.
* Dr. Adeyemi concluded that immediate market withdrawal is not clinically warranted at this juncture, provided that operative instructions and risks regarding component positioning are communicated with heightened clarity to operating surgeons.

4. DISCUSSION & REGULATORY DETERMINATION
The committee reviewed potential courses of action: voluntary market withdrawal versus commercial continuation accompanied by targeted risk mitigation (labeling modifications and formal clinician notification).

* M. Lee and C. Mendes emphasized that commercial partners and clinical key opinion leaders require immediate guidance to prevent misinterpretation of NJR data in the field, noting the commercial disruption of a full withdrawal without definitive surgical positioning guidance.
* D. Okonkwo and P. Raman advised that regulatory standards permit commercial continuation under a controlled risk mitigation strategy, provided that the FDA is notified of significant labeling updates and that complaint trending under 21 CFR 820.198 continues with increased surveillance frequency.
* Decision: Following consensus discussion, the committee determined to continue global distribution and sales of the ApexHip system, contingent upon an expedited labeling update highlighting cup inclination limitations and the issuance of an urgent clinician notification letter ("Dear Doctor" letter).
* Executive Concurrence: R. Castellano confirmed executive agreement with the recommended approach, noting that surgeon education and precise placement parameters represent the appropriate, measured path forward.

5. ACTION ITEMS

| Action Item | Assignee | Target Date |
|:---|:---|:---|
| 1. Draft formal 510(k) labeling update submission emphasizing strict acetabular cup inclination tolerances (target ≤45°) and enhanced warnings regarding metal-on-metal adverse reactions. | D. Okonkwo | October 1, 2021 |
| 2. Draft comprehensive "Dear Doctor" communication outlining registry observations, proper patient selection, and intraoperative positioning precautions for surgeon distribution. | C. Mendes / Dr. L. Adeyemi | September 28, 2021 |
| 3. Establish bi-weekly complaint trending protocols and explant analysis monitoring within TrackWise for all incoming ApexHip metal-ion and revision reports. | P. Raman | September 21, 2021 |
| 4. Maintain ongoing data reconciliation with AJRR working groups to track domestic revision velocity. | G. Novak | November 15, 2021 |

6. ADJOURNMENT
The meeting was formally adjourned at 11:45 AM.

*Minutes respectfully submitted by:*
Devon Mitchell, Sr. Regulatory Specialist
*Approved by:* Dana Okonkwo, VP Regulatory Affairs (September 15, 2021)

TO: Executive Leadership Team
FROM: Lisa Tran, HR Business Partner, R&D and Quality
DATE: February 5, 2024
SUBJECT: Workforce Transition Plan - ApexHip Market Withdrawal

Following the February 2, 2024 announcement regarding the voluntary global market withdrawal of the ApexHip Total Hip System, Human Resources has finalized the workforce transition and organizational alignment plan.

While this market action impacts product line revenue and commercial focus, our regulatory, clinical, and quality obligations for previously implanted units remain fully active. Consequently, this plan balances necessary commercial consolidation with targeted personnel retention across technical operations.

1. Scope of Impacted Personnel

The withdrawal directly impacts positions dedicated exclusively to the commercialization, promotional positioning, and field support of ApexHip:

• Commercial Sales: Five (5) Regional Reconstruction Specialists whose sole portfolio assignment was ApexHip conversion accounts across the Southeast, Central, and Western territories. General reconstructive sales representatives carrying KneeFlex and shoulder lines will absorb remaining territory accounts and are unaffected by this reduction.
• Marketing Communications: Four (4) dedicated contractor roles within MarCom supporting Apex product campaigns, digital asset management, and agency liaison work (Kessler Reid deliverables). Contracts will be concluded effective February 29, 2024, per standard notice provisions.
• Operations / Field Inventory: Two (2) logistics coordinator roles in Warsaw supporting hospital consignment retrieval and field kit balancing.

2. Retention of Core Technical, Quality, and Regulatory Staff

It is critical to emphasize that no headcount reductions will occur within Product Development, Regulatory Affairs, Post-Market Surveillance, or Quality Complaint Handling.

Per 21 CFR 820 and 803 requirements, our post-market surveillance, adverse event trending, and complaint investigation responsibilities continue indefinitely for all legacy implanted ApexHip systems. The following teams will remain intact:

• Quality & Complaint Handling: Priya Raman’s team will maintain current staffing levels to manage incoming TrackWise complaint files, MDR determinations, and explant evaluations.
• Post-Market Surveillance: Greg Novak will continue overseeing registry monitoring (AJRR, NJR), signal detection, and ongoing surveillance reports.
• R&D Engineering: Lead sustaining engineer Wei Chen and supporting mechanical testing staff will remain fully allocated to ongoing retrieval analyses, wear simulator evaluations, and technical support for ongoing regulatory inquiries.

3. Severance and Transition Package Terms

For eligible regular full-time employees subject to position elimination, Veridian will offer standard severance packages structured as follows:

• Base Severance: Two (2) weeks of base pay per year of continuous service, with a minimum of eight (8) weeks and a maximum of twenty-six (26) weeks.
• Benefits Continuation: Employer-subsidized COBRA premium coverage corresponding to the severance duration period.
• Incentive Compensation: Pro-rated FY2024 target bonus payouts calculated through March 31, 2024.
• Outplacement Services: Three (3) months of executive and professional outplacement assistance via Lee Hecht Harrison (LHH).

4. Implementation Timeline

• Feb 5–Feb 9: Finalize Workday role status updates; prepare individualized separation documentation and release agreements with outside legal review.
• Feb 12–Feb 16: Manager briefing sessions; coordinate notification scheduling with VP Sales Marcus Lee and relevant regional directors.
• Feb 19–Feb 23: Conduct individual notification meetings with impacted commercial staff.
• Feb 29: Contract conclusion date for MarCom external contractors.
• March 29, 2024: Target final separation date for impacted regular employees.

Please direct any questions regarding specific employee conversations or Workday processing directly to me.

MEMORANDUM

Date: October 12, 2018
From: Tom Halvorsen, Sr. Design Engineer
Subject: KneeFlex Design FMEA - Rev 1

This memo documents the first formal design FMEA for the KneeFlex tibial insert, tibial tray interface, femoral component, and associated trialing instrumentation. This revision incorporates the bench findings from the August build and the usability observations from the Warsaw cadaver lab. The worksheet is being routed with the Rev 1 design package and will be updated after completion of the fatigue and simulator protocols.

The intent here is to identify reasonably foreseeable component and instrument failures before design verification is locked. Scores use the standard Veridian 1–10 scale for Severity (S), Occurrence (O), and Detection (D). Risk Priority Number (RPN) is S x O x D. Items at or above 120 require a documented mitigation or rationale before the next design review.

| Item / Failure Mode | Potential Effect | S | Potential Cause | O | Current Controls / Detection | D | RPN |
|---|---|---:|---|---:|---|---:|---:|
| Polyethylene tibial insert wear above expected rate | Osteolysis, pain, early revision | 8 | Inadequate resin processing; elevated contact stress in deep flexion | 4 | Resin certification; dimensional inspection; simulator test planned | 5 | 160 |
| Tibial insert locking feature fatigue or disengagement | Insert micromotion, instability, debris generation | 9 | Repeated posterior loading; tolerance stack between insert and tray | 3 | Locking-force test; cyclic fatigue test in development | 5 | 135 |
| Femoral component cementless surface insufficient for fixation | Migration, pain, revision procedure | 9 | Porosity variation; inadequate surface preparation | 3 | Coating thickness inspection; pull-off samples; radiographic migration protocol planned | 4 | 108 |
| Femoral component fracture | Loss of function, revision surgery | 10 | Material defect; undersized component in high-load patient | 1 | Material lot certification; finite element analysis; fatigue test | 4 | 40 |
| Tibial tray post deformation | Insert instability or altered kinematics | 8 | High cyclic load at post base; machining variation | 2 | Dimensional inspection; bench fatigue test | 5 | 80 |
| Trial inserter or extraction instrument breakage | Extended operative time; possible retained fragment | 7 | Instrument shaft overload; repeated reprocessing; improper engagement | 3 | Torque specification; cadaver-lab inspection; instrument fatigue test | 5 | 105 |

The highest initial RPN is insert wear. This is not unexpected for a mobile-bearing-adjacent design, although KneeFlex is a fixed-bearing system. The issue is not the nominal wear result; it is the sensitivity of the design to alignment and to the backside contact pattern if the insert is not fully seated. The current simulator plan includes neutral alignment and a malalignment condition. I recommend adding a deliberately incomplete seating condition to the bench protocol rather than assuming the locking click is sufficient confirmation in all cases. Manufacturing should also retain molding and irradiation records by insert lot for the verification builds.

The locking mechanism is the next item needing work. In the August build, two inserts showed visible witness marking along the anterior rail after repeated removal and reinsertion. Neither disengaged, but the force-to-remove values dropped after the tenth cycle. That may be an artifact of the prototype machining, but we should not treat it as one until the production-intent tray and insert are tested together. The proposed control is to establish a minimum retention force and maximum insertion force specification, then confirm both after cyclic loading.

For the femoral component, the current concern is less fracture than fixation consistency. The porous surface process is still being finalized with Cork, and the coupon data are acceptable but limited. We need production-representative coupons before closing this line item. The severity remains high because a fixation failure is clinically significant even if the expected occurrence is low.

Instrument breakage was raised by two surgeons during the cadaver lab, specifically when the trial extraction tool was used at an angle rather than inline with the tray. The current design has insufficient margin for that use condition. Engineering will evaluate a larger shaft diameter and a revised engagement geometry. Training language alone is not an adequate control if the instrument predictably sees off-axis loading in surgery.

Actions before the next design review:

1. Add incomplete-insert-seating and deep-flexion conditions to the wear and locking verification protocol.
2. Define acceptance criteria for locking retention force following cyclic loading and repeated instrument use.
3. Obtain production-intent coating coupons and process capability information from Cork.
4. Redesign the trial extraction instrument interface and repeat the cadaver-lab evaluation.
5. Re-score the FMEA after verification results are available and document any residual risk rationale.

Tom Halvorsen
Sr. Design Engineer, Knee Reconstruction

This document is confidential and should be retained in the employee's personnel file per standard Workday HR record retention procedure.

Background

During inspection-readiness review conducted the week of June 14, 2021, Quality identified a backlog of 47 open complaints in TrackWise assigned to Ms. Ferro's queue, several of which exceeded internal timeliness targets for MDR reportability determination. Per procedure QP-0091, reportability decisions are expected within 5 business days of complaint receipt, and complaint files are expected to close within 30 days absent documented extension. Ms. Ferro's queue showed a median time-to-decision of 14 business days over the prior quarter, and multiple files remained open beyond 45 days without documented justification. This contributed to one of the three observations noted informally by the inspection team regarding complaint trending timeliness, and is a significant compliance concern given 21 CFR 803 obligations.

Performance Expectations — 60-Day Plan (August 2 – October 1, 2021)

1. Reduce open TrackWise queue from 47 to fewer than 15 complaints within the first 30 days, and to a steady-state working queue thereafter.
2. Meet the 5-business-day reportability determination target on 100% of new complaints assigned during the plan period.
3. Close 90% of complaint files within 30 days per procedure, with any exception documented and approved by Ms. Raman in advance.
4. No missed or late MDR submissions during the plan period.

Support and Check-Ins

Ms. Raman will conduct weekly one-on-one check-ins (Mondays, 30 minutes) to review queue status, discuss any files at risk of missing timeliness targets, and provide coaching. HR will participate in a check-in at the 30-day mark to assess progress. Additional TrackWise refresher training has been scheduled for the week of August 9.

Consequences

Failure to meet the metrics above by the end of the 60-day period, or any new instance of a late MDR determination during the plan period, may result in further disciplinary action up to and including termination of employment, consistent with Veridian's performance management policy.

Acknowledgment

Ms. Ferro will be asked to sign acknowledging receipt of this plan; signature does not indicate agreement with its contents, only that the plan has been reviewed and discussed.

Leon

Subject: Engineering Status Review: ECO-2019-118 (Apex Acetabular Cup Rim Geometry & Clearance) — Closing the Loop

MEMORANDUM

TO: Priya Raman, Director of Quality & Complaint Handling; Carlos Mendes, Product Manager, ApexHip
FROM: Tom Halvorsen, Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip
DATE: January 10, 2022
SUBJECT: Engineering Status Review: ECO-2019-118 (Apex Acetabular Cup Rim Geometry & Clearance) — Closing the Loop

I am writing to formally revisit the open engineering posture surrounding ECO-2019-118. It has now been nearly three years since I submitted the initial Engineering Change Order proposal in February 2019, and our Design History File (DHF) index still does not accurately capture where we stand on this.

To recap the technical history: during the development phase leading up to Design Review 3 (DR-3) in November 2016, our wear simulator protocol was established strictly under ISO 14242-1 standard parameters, testing acetabular component placement at a nominal 45° inclination angle only. The Meridian Testing Labs reports confirmed acceptable volumetric wear under those ideal, nominal conditions, which supported our 510(k) clearance (K162447). However, as I flagged in my February 2019 re-analysis memo, testing the system under steeper acetabular cup inclinations—specifically 55°—produced severe edge-loading dynamics. The wear simulator data showed a 4× to 6× increase in gravimetric and volumetric metal wear rates compared to the 45° baseline, driven by localized contact stresses at the cup rim during microseparation cycles.

ECO-2019-118 proposed an immediate modification to the acetabular rim radius and polar clearance profile to mitigate edge-loading wear at non-ideal cup angles (which clinical data shows occur frequently in real-world patient anatomy).

In mid-2019, leadership decided to formally defer ECO-2019-118. The stated rationale at the time centered on commercial friction: tooling changeout costs, scrap write-downs, and especially the timeline required for full mechanical and simulator requalification, which would have disrupted peak production volumes.

Here is my primary concern today: as of January 2022, three full years after we identified the 4–6× wear multiplier under steep angles, no design change has been implemented. None. The product currently being shipped from Warsaw and Cork retains the exact rim geometry cleared in 2017.

Furthermore, I reviewed the ApexHip DHF index in Agile last week and noticed ECO-2019-118 is marked as "Closed / Superseded by Commercial Labeling Review." This is factually incorrect and creates an audit vulnerability. The engineering risk was never resolved or designed out; it was *deferred*. We should not be relying solely on post-market technique guides or surgeon education to manage a mechanical wear condition that we know occurs once the cup tilts past 50°.

I recommend two immediate corrective actions:
1. Re-open the DHF index entry for ECO-2019-118 and formally designate its status as "Deferred — Pending Clinical Registry / Post-Market Review," explicitly noting that the original ISO 14242 protocol tested only 45° inclination and did not evaluate edge-loading conditions.
2. Reconvene the cross-functional engineering review team (Quality, Product Management, R&D) to decide whether we are going to requalify the modified rim tooling or leave the deferred status on the permanent record.

We have known about the edge-loading wear multiplier since early 2019. Leaving the change order in administrative limbo without a clear engineering resolution is a significant unaddressed risk.

Regards,

Tom Halvorsen
Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip
Veridian Orthopedics, Inc.

FINANCIAL PLANNING & ANALYSIS
MEMORANDUM / SPREADSHEET SUMMARY

TO: Owen Park, Chief Financial Officer
FROM: Hannah Berg, FP&A Manager
DATE: July 14, 2020
SUBJECT: ClassicHip Finished Goods Inventory Aging & Proposed Write-Down Analysis

Owen,

Per our discussion last week regarding the continued operational phase-out of the ClassicHip system, I have finalized the aging analysis of our remaining finished-goods inventory held across Warsaw central distribution and the four regional hubs (Atlanta, Dallas, Denver, Newark).

Given that commercial demand for ClassicHip has dropped another 42% year-over-year as surgical volume transitioned away from metal-on-polyethylene lines, our current inventory levels significantly exceed projected trailing demand through the scheduled 2022 product retirement date.

Based on our standard excess and obsolete (E&O) policy for product lines under formal phase-out schedules, I am recommending an inventory write-down of $1,185,400 for Q3 close.

ClassicHip Inventory Valuation & Proposed Reserve (as of June 30, 2020)

| SKU Category | Active Lots (<12 mos) | Aging (12–24 mos) | Stagnant (>24 mos) | Total Extended Cost | Proposed Write-Down |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Classic Acetabular Cups (sizes 44–60mm) | $184,200 | $312,800 | $440,100 | $937,100 | $485,200 |
| Classic Femoral Stems (Standard/Lateral) | $210,500 | $285,400 | $398,000 | $893,900 | $412,600 |
| Co/Cr Modular Heads (28–36mm) | $98,400 | $174,200 | $262,900 | $535,500 | $287,600 |
| Total ClassicHip FG Inventory | $493,100 | $772,400 | $1,101,000 | $2,366,500 | $1,185,400 |

*Notes:*

Date: April 1, 2022
Distribution: Devon Mitchell; Greg Novak
Product: ApexHip Metal-on-Metal Total Hip System
Reporting Period: January 1–March 31, 2022
Subject: Q1 2022 metal-ion complaint trending summary

Per the complaint-trending procedure, Quality reviewed all ApexHip complaints closed or opened during Q1 2022 with reported elevated cobalt and/or chromium values, suspected ARMD, tissue reaction, or revision associated with metal debris. Duplicate reports concerning the same patient event were consolidated where identifiable.

A total of 19 metal-ion-related ApexHip complaints were recorded during Q1 2022, compared with 12 during Q1 2021. The increase is concentrated in territories where the product has historically had greater utilization and where follow-up laboratory values are being obtained more consistently.

| Region | Q1 2022 Complaints | Revision Outcome Reported |
|---|---:|---:|
| Southeast | 7 | 5 |
| Nashville | 4 | 3 |
| Denver | 3 | 2 |
| Other | 5 | 4 |
| Total | 19 | 14 |

Of the 19 complaints, 14 include confirmation that revision surgery occurred or had been scheduled based on the latest information provided by the treating facility or surgeon. The remaining five reports involve ongoing surveillance, imaging, repeat laboratory testing, or a recommendation for clinical follow-up. Complaint files remain subject to update as additional operative and explant information is received.

Serum cobalt values were available in 16 of the 19 complaint records. The average reported serum cobalt level among those complainants was 41 ppb. This is materially above the generally cited normal range of less than 1 ppb in individuals without a cobalt-containing implant. Chromium values were also elevated in a majority of records, although reporting units and collection timing were not uniform enough to calculate a comparable aggregate without further normalization.

The observed trend continues to track with the pattern Halvorsen’s engineering team identified in prior wear testing, including increased wear under non-standard cup positioning conditions. Quality is continuing to process each event per procedure, including MDR assessment where applicable, and will provide the underlying TrackWise extract to Regulatory and PMS for their respective review.

VERIDIAN ORTHOPEDICS, INC.
Internal Memorandum

Date: February 11, 2019
From: Tom Halvorsen, Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip
To: Priya Raman, Director, Quality & Complaint Handling
Carlos Mendes, Product Manager, ApexHip
Subject: ApexHip wear re-test results at 55 degree inclination

Priya, Carlos —

Wanted to get this in front of you before I go any further with it, because I don't love what I'm seeing.

Back at DR-3 in 2016 we locked the wear-test protocol at 45 degrees inclination only, per ISO 14242, and that's what's been in the DHF ever since. I've been sitting on a hunch since last fall that we should be checking off-nominal cup positioning too, since that's closer to what actually happens in a lot of real hips depending on surgical technique. So I had Meridian Labs re-run the protocol at 55 degrees cup inclination on a fresh set of cup/head pairs, same lot family as production, same head material (Co/Cr on Co/Cr).

Results are in — Meridian report MTL-19-0142, dated 2/6/19. Raw numbers:

- 45° inclination (standard, matches our cleared data): ~2.1 mm3 per million cycles volumetric wear, consistent with what we submitted in the 510(k).
- 55° inclination: ~9.8–12.4 mm3 per million cycles, depending on the sample. That's 4 to 6x higher than standard angle.

This is not subtle. The wear scar pattern on the cup rim at 55° is exactly the edge-loading signature I flagged in my concept-phase notes back in 2015 when we were still finalizing head/cup clearance tolerances — I'd predicted this could happen at high inclination but we didn't build it into the formal test matrix because ISO 14242 doesn't require it and DR-3 decided standard angle was sufficient for clearance purposes. In hindsight I think that was the wrong call, or at least an incomplete one.

I know this is a MoM system, so wear debris isn't just a mechanical problem — it's a Co/Cr ion generation problem, and higher wear volume at higher inclination is going to mean higher ion release in patients who end up with cups sitting steep, whether that's from surgical variability or from cup design geometry not tolerating it well.

Priya — has TrackWise flagged anything that could line up with this? I'm thinking about the Atlanta cluster from last August, three patients out of Feld's practice. I don't have visibility into implant positioning on those cases but if any of them were high-inclination placements this could be more than coincidence.

I want to be careful here — this is one lab run, small sample, and I haven't done the statistics properly yet (need to look at variance across the sample set before I say anything definitive). But the magnitude is big enough that I think we need to start looking seriously at either a design change to cup geometry (bigger clearance angle tolerance, maybe a modified rim profile) or reconsidering head material/size combinations to reduce edge-loading sensitivity.

Can we get 20 minutes this week to talk through next steps? I'd rather we get ahead of this than have it come up some other way.

Tom

Design History File — Engineering Memorandum

Date: 2 April 2019
From: Tom Halvorsen, Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip
Subject: Design Change Rationale — ECO-2019-118 (Cup Rim Geometry)
Distribution: DHF file copy; cc Priya Raman, Carlos Mendes

1. Purpose

This memo documents the technical basis for proposed engineering change order ECO-2019-118, which would modify the acetabular cup rim geometry on ApexHip to reduce edge-loading wear observed at higher cup inclination angles. It also records the current disposition of the change.

2. Background

Per DR-3 (Nov 2016), the wear-test protocol adopted for ApexHip design verification used ISO 14242 methodology at a fixed 45° cup inclination angle only. That was consistent with prevailing industry practice for MoM bearings at the time and was reviewed and approved by the design review board. No testing was performed at higher inclination angles during original verification.

In Feb 2019 I re-ran wear testing (Meridian Testing Labs, report attached as Apex_wear_55deg_rev2.xlsx) at 55° inclination to evaluate performance under conditions more representative of real-world cup positioning variability, prompted by field data patterns I'd been informally tracking. Results showed volumetric wear rates 4-6x higher than the 45° baseline, consistent with an edge-loading mechanism at the cup rim under elevated inclination. This is a materially different wear regime than what our original verification testing characterized.

I flagged these results to Priya Raman and Carlos Mendes in Feb 2019 (see my 2/14/19 memo). This ECO is the engineering follow-up.

3. Proposed Change

ECO-2019-118 would modify the cup rim profile (increased rim coverage/reduced chamfer angle) to reduce the incidence and severity of edge loading at inclination angles above the 45° baseline, without materially changing head diameter compatibility or the KinetiCoat ingrowth surface.

4. Alternatives Considered

a. Full redesign of rim geometry per above — addresses root mechanism directly but requires new tooling and re-verification.
b. No hardware change; instead issue supplemental surgical technique guidance to surgeons emphasizing target cup inclination angle (recommend tightening guidance toward 40-45° with instrumentation aids) to reduce the incidence of high-inclination placements in the field.
c. No action — not recommended; field inclination variability is well documented in the literature and cannot be assumed to trend toward the 45° baseline on its own.

5. Cost and Timeline (Option a)

Tooling changes for the modified rim profile are estimated at $2.1M, primarily new injection/machining tooling at Cork plus revalidation. Estimated timeline to implementation is approximately 9 months, including design verification testing at both 45° and 55° inclination, updated FMEA, and a supplemental 510(k) or letter-to-file determination pending regulatory review.

6. Recommendation

I recommend pursuing either (a) the rim redesign or, at minimum, (b) updated surgical technique guidance as an interim mitigation while a redesign is evaluated. Given the magnitude of the wear multiplier at 55°, I don't think no-action is defensible from an engineering standpoint, though I recognize the clinical significance of this lab-scale finding relative to actual field revision rates is still an open question.

7. Disposition

This change has been discussed with Quality and Product Management. Per direction from management, ECO-2019-118 is deferred at this time pending additional clinical correlation data (i.e., whether registry/complaint trends support a wear-driven revision signal sufficient to justify the tooling investment and field guidance change). This memo and the underlying test data are retained in the DHF for future reference should the ECO be reopened.

Tom Halvorsen
Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip

Attendees: Greg Novak (Post-Market Surveillance), Dana Okonkwo (Regulatory Affairs), Priya Raman (Quality & Complaint Handling), Dr. Leon Adeyemi (CMO)

1. Purpose
This meeting was a scheduled follow-up to the September 14, 2021 Registry Signal Review, to check whether newer registry data changes the picture that led to the decision to continue selling ApexHip with the labeling update and October 2021 Dear Doctor letter.

2. AJRR Q4 2021 Data (Novak)
Novak presented late-2021 AJRR figures. Revision rates for ApexHip remain elevated relative to the broader class average, consistent in direction and magnitude with the March 2021 NJR finding of a 7.1% five-year revision rate versus a 3.2% class average. Novak noted the AJRR dataset has a shorter follow-up window than NJR but the trend line is not moving in a favorable direction quarter over quarter. He cautioned against over-reading a single quarter but said two consecutive registries now point the same way.

3. Discussion — Is the Current Response Sufficient?
Okonkwo asked whether the label update and surgeon letter constitute an adequate response given the AJRR confirmation, or whether the company should revisit a design change (referencing the ECO-2019-118 proposal that was deferred in 2019) or a temporary sales pause pending further analysis.

Raman noted that complaint volumes in TrackWise have not shown a corresponding spike since the Dear Doctor letter went out, but acknowledged this could reflect underreporting or a lag rather than resolution.

Adeyemi stated that from a clinical standpoint the registry signal is concerning but that causation relative to surgical technique (inclination angle) versus device design has not been definitively separated, and that a sales pause is a significant step that should not be taken on registry data alone without further wear-testing correlation.

There was general discussion of the anticipated litigation hold, expected to be entered February 1, 2022, following Whitfield & Barr's engagement in January. The group agreed this development increases the importance of being able to show the company is actively monitoring and reassessing, but did not treat it as changing the substantive risk analysis.

4. Decision
No decision was made to alter the current course of action. The label update and Dear Doctor letter remain the company's position for now. The group agreed to revisit at the next quarterly review or sooner if AJRR or NJR data worsens materially.

- Novak to prepare updated registry trend charts (NJR/AJRR combined view) for inclusion in the next board pre-read.
- Raman to continue monthly complaint trending and flag any deviation.

MEMORANDUM

TO: ApexHip Design History File (DHF-0042)
FROM: Tom Halvorsen, Sr. Design Engineer, Reconstructive R&D
DATE: March 22, 2019
SUBJECT: Design Change Evaluation – ECO-2019-118 (Acetabular Cup Sub-Hemispherical Geometry Modification) – DEFERRED STATUS
CC: Priya Raman, Director of Quality; Carlos Mendes, Product Manager; Dana Okonkwo, VP Regulatory Affairs

1. Purpose
This memorandum documents the technical review, simulator wear-testing results, and final disposition rationale for Engineering Change Order ECO-2019-118 regarding the ApexHip Total Hip System. Under 21 CFR 820.30(i), this record captures the engineering evaluation and formal decision to defer the proposed design modification.

2. Background and Proposed Change
ECO-2019-118 was initiated in January 2019 to evaluate potential cup modifications intended to reduce edge-loading phenomena under steep cup placement. The proposed change comprised a 1.2 mm reduction in cup coverage angle and an increased rim blend radius across sizes 44–62 mm to broaden the functional safe zone during micro-separation and steep operative inclination.

3. Simulator Wear-Testing Summary
Initial pre-market clearance wear testing was conducted by Meridian Testing Labs in 2016 per ISO 14242-1 standard parameters (45° inclination angle, 1.0–2.0 mm head offset). Under this standard protocol, the ApexHip system demonstrated low volumetric wear rates compatible with cleared predicate performance:
* Report MT-2016-0882: *ISO 14242-1 ApexHip 45° Wear Simulator 5.0 Mc Cycle Testing* (Meridian Testing Labs, final report dated November 14, 2016). Mean steady-state wear rate: 0.82 mm³/Mc.

In February 2019, R&D contracted supplemental simulator wear testing at an elevated inclination angle of 55° to assess wear kinetics under non-ideal surgical alignment and extreme biomechanical positioning:
* Report MT-2019-0144: *ApexHip Kinematic Wear Characterization at Steep Inclination (55°)* (Meridian Testing Labs, final report dated February 18, 2019).

The 55° protocol demonstrated a pronounced escalation in metallic wear, showing a 4× to 6× increase in volumetric wear rate (mean steady-state wear rate: 4.65 mm³/Mc) compared to the standard 45° setup. Gravimetric analysis and laser surface profilometry confirmed that steep orientation induces localized contact stress spikes along the superior rim, resulting in edge-loading and rim stripe wear.

4. Rationale for Deferral
On March 8, 2019, an engineering and product cross-functional review convened to evaluate ECO-2019-118. The decision was reached to defer implementation based on the following considerations:

1. Limited Clinical Correlation: ISO 14242-1 at 45° remains the recognized consensus standard for total hip replacement testing. Elevated angles (55°) represent severe boundary conditions that exceed typical surgical alignment targets (Lewinnek safe zone: 40° ± 10°). At present, post-market surveillance data (TrackWise) does not show a verified in vivo correlation between the steep bench simulation and active customer complaint trends.
2. Requalification and Re-clearing Burden: Tooling re-qualification across the full shell matrix (sizes 44–62 mm), updated validation runs at Cork, and potential 510(k) supplementary filings would involve significant resource allocation and lead times (estimated 12–16 months), which is not warranted absent a confirmed clinical failure mechanism.
3. Surveillance Strategy: Rather than redesigning the implant geometry based on extreme simulator parameters, the team determined that post-market monitoring is the appropriate risk control. R&D and Quality will actively track domestic and international arthroplasty registry data, specifically monitoring revision signals from the National Joint Registry (NJR) of England and Wales and the American Joint Replacement Registry (AJRR).

5. Conclusion and Review Cycle
ECO-2019-118 is formally placed in DEFERRED status in Agile PLM. This design change evaluation will be revisited annually during management review or immediately upon identification of a confirmed clinical or registry signal indicating adverse wear performance in the field.

Tom Halvorsen
Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip
Veridian Orthopedics, Inc.

THIS DOCUMENT LISTS OBSERVATIONS MADE BY THE FDA REPRESENTATIVE(S) DURING THE INSPECTION OF YOUR FACILITY. THEY ARE INSPECTIONAL OBSERVATIONS; AND DO NOT REPRESENT A FINAL AGENCY DETERMINATION REGARDING YOUR COMPLIANCE. IF YOU HAVE AN OBJECTION REGARDING AN OBSERVATION, OR HAVE IMPLEMENTED, OR PLAN TO IMPLEMENT, CORRECTIVE ACTION IN RESPONSE TO AN OBSERVATION, YOU MAY DISCUSS THE OBJECTION OR ACTION WITH THE FDA REPRESENTATIVE(S) DURING THE INSPECTION OR SUBMIT THIS INFORMATION TO FDA AT THE ADDRESS ABOVE.

DURING AN INSPECTION OF YOUR FIRM (LOCATED AT WARSAW, INDIANA) ON JUNE 14 THROUGH JUNE 21, 2021, THE FOLLOWING OBSERVATIONS WERE NOTED:

OBSERVATION 1
Procedures for receiving, reviewing, and evaluating complaints have not been adequately established and maintained, as required by 21 CFR 820.198(a).

Specifically, post-market complaint analysis and trending procedures (SOP-QA-408, "Post-Market Surveillance and Trend Analysis," Rev. 4) were not implemented in a timely manner. Your firm failed to escalate statistically significant upward trends in revision-related complaint files associated with the ApexHip Total Hip System to executive management review. Specifically, TrackWise complaint records logged between October 2020 and April 2021 citing early femoral head/acetabular cup revision, pain, and adverse tissue reactions were not evaluated against historical baseline thresholds established in your Quality Plan, resulting in an unmitigated delay of over six months in escalating post-market revision signals to the Corrective and Preventive Action (CAPA) board and executive leadership.

OBSERVATION 2
Corrective and preventive actions have not been fully documented, as required by 21 CFR 820.100(b).

Specifically, CAPA-2020-088, initiated regarding dimensional variances during CNC machining of hip stems, was closed on January 15, 2021, without verification or validation demonstrating that the corrective actions taken were effective and did not adversely affect the finished device.

OBSERVATION 3
Personnel are not adequately trained to perform their assigned responsibilities, as required by 21 CFR 820.25(b).

Specifically, training records for three of twelve quality assurance technicians responsible for review and disposition of incoming component inspection records lacked documentation of annual re-qualification training on sampling standard SOP-QC-102.

ANNUAL PERFORMANCE REVIEW — FY2022

Employee: Greg Novak
Title: Director, Post-Market Surveillance
Department: Quality / Regulatory Affairs
Manager: Dana Okonkwo
Reviewer/HR Partner: Lisa Tran
Review Period: January 1, 2022 – December 31, 2022
Date Prepared: February 10, 2023

Overall Rating: Exceeds Expectations

1. Summary of Performance

Greg had a strong year. His core responsibility — monitoring registry data (NJR, AJRR) and internal complaint trends for early signal detection — continued to be a high point of his performance, building on the analytical groundwork he laid in 2021. Dana and I both heard consistent feedback from Quality and Regulatory leadership that Greg's registry work is thorough, well-documented, and delivered on time even when the underlying data sets are messy or delayed from the registry administrators. His March 2021 NJR analysis (flagging the ApexHip 5-year revision rate) and the follow-on AJRR review later that year were cited by more than one manager this cycle as foundational to the company's understanding of the signal, and Greg's slide decks and memos from that period are still referenced in current discussions.

It's worth noting for the file that Greg's role in the September 2021 Registry Signal Review was limited to analysis and presentation of the data; the resulting business decision (to continue commercialization with a labeling update) was made by senior leadership and is outside the scope of Greg's individual performance. Greg has, appropriately, kept his focus on data integrity and surfacing signals rather than advocacy for a particular outcome, which several colleagues specifically praised as a mark of professionalism.

2. Strengths

- Deep registry expertise (NJR, AJRR); go-to person for surveillance methodology questions across Quality and RA.
- Clear, well-organized written analysis; decks are described as "board-ready" by more than one stakeholder.
- Reliable under deadline pressure, including around FDA inspection response support in mid-2022.
- Collaborative with Priya Raman's complaint-handling team on cross-referencing registry signals against TrackWise trends.

3. Areas for Development

- Greg has acknowledged that a meaningful portion of his AJRR data handling is still manual (spreadsheet-based pulls and reconciliation), which creates bottlenecks and some risk of transcription error as data volumes grow.
- Could delegate more routine trending work to build bench strength on his small team.

4. 2023 Goals

- Lead an initiative to automate AJRR data ingestion and reconciliation, reducing manual spreadsheet work and turnaround time for quarterly trend reports.
- Formalize a documented registry-monitoring SOP with defined escalation thresholds.
- Cross-train one additional team member on NJR/AJRR methodology.
- Continue supporting Regulatory and Quality on post-market surveillance deliverables as needed.

5. Compensation/Advancement Note

Given the "Exceeds Expectations" rating, Greg is recommended for a merit increase per the FY2023 compensation bands; details to be finalized separately with Dana and Compensation.

Rachel,

Attached is the draft 21 CFR Part 806 recall notification package prepared for submission to CDRH regarding the voluntary recall of ApexHip acetabular cups.

Per our discussion with Bill Kowalski and Quality, the key elements summarized in the submission document are as follows:

1. Root Cause: Adhesion failure of the porous titanium KinetiCoat layer attributed to plasma-spray parameter drift following scheduled vacuum chamber maintenance at the Cork facility.
2. Scope / Lot Range: Acetabular cup lots V-2200 through V-2299, manufactured in Cork between November 2021 and February 2022.
3. Distribution Data: 1,140 total units distributed commercially; based on hospital reconciliation and registry cross-referencing to date, 412 units have been implanted.
4. Health Hazard Evaluation & Classification: Proposing a voluntary Class II classification. The risk assessment concludes that while unbonded coating flaking upon opening presents a delay in surgery or potential local inflammatory response if introduced, the probability of serious adverse health consequences remains low.

We are targeting an official submission date to the FDA district office in early June, prior to the planned formal customer notification and initiation date of June 14, 2022.

Summary of Performance

Devon had a demanding year, much of it shaped by the ongoing regulatory activity surrounding ApexHip. He continued to own the MDR filing calendar for the group, and I can say without reservation that his tracking discipline is one of the more reliable parts of our reporting infrastructure. Per the 21 CFR 803 timeliness requirements, we did not miss a single filing deadline this period despite a meaningfully higher volume of reportable events tied to Apex complaints during Q3 and Q4. Apex Revenue Impact Model — Q4 2022 Scenarios
Prepared by: Hannah Berg, FP&A Manager
Date: October 14, 2022
To: Owen Park, CFO
Subject: Apex Revenue Impact Model - Q4 2022 Scenarios

Attached: `Apex_Revenue_Impact_Model_Q4_2022_v5.xlsx`

Owen,

Per our discussion, I refreshed the Apex model using September actuals and the current field forecast. The model is intended to frame revenue exposure through FY24; it does not attempt to estimate claim severity or timing.

Apex FY22 is now expected to close at approximately $71.0M, versus the $96.0M peak in FY20. The decline began before the June cup recall in the underlying order data. The more pronounced step-down follows the September 2021 labeling update and what Sales characterizes as increased surgeon caution after the NJR data circulated. The recall remains a separate, lot-specific assumption in the model, although several field teams report customers are not making that distinction.

Summary output ($M):

| Scenario | FY22E | FY23E | FY24E | FY22–FY24 Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Status quo / current label | 71.0 | 62.4 | 60.1 | (15%) |
| Label-driven decline | 71.0 | 54.7 | 45.9 | (35%) |
| Full market withdrawal | 71.0 | 48.3 | 42.6 | (40%) |

The status quo case assumes current labeling remains in place, no broad commercial action, and modest attrition offset by existing account utilization. It is the closest to the current Sales operating plan, though I would not characterize it as the base case with high confidence.

The label-driven decline case assumes continued loss of new implanters, lower utilization among accounts that have moved Apex to a limited-use position, and increasing price concessions where distributors seek to retain volume. This case reflects the present trajectory in the Southeast and selected Midwest accounts more closely than the operating plan.

The withdrawal case assumes no new commercial placements after an orderly market action, with only limited residual revenue from contracted inventory and replacement requirements. This is necessarily a planning construct, not a recommendation regarding product status.

For reserve adequacy testing, I recommend using the full withdrawal scenario as the conservative revenue sensitivity. It produces the lowest contribution available to absorb claims-related costs and avoids relying on a recovery in surgeon confidence that we are not seeing in the current forecast submissions.

I have kept the $18M Q3 reserve as a separate line item in the workbook and have not assumed any insurance recoveries. We can walk through the account-level assumptions Monday if helpful.

Hannah

Date: August 15, 2022
Prepared by: Lisa Tran, HR Business Partner, R&D and Quality
Subject: Mid-Year Check-in - Tom Halvorsen

I met with Tom on August 11 as part of the informal mid-year check-in cycle for the ApexHip engineering group. This was not a formal performance review and no action is required in Workday at this time.

Tom continues to perform strongly in his Senior Design Engineer role. His technical knowledge of the Apex system, including historical design decisions, wear-testing methodology, and supporting DHF documentation, remains unusually deep. His manager reports that he is responsive on technical questions, thorough with data review, and dependable when cross-functional teams need historical context. Tom has also been helpful to newer engineers who are trying to understand the legacy KBT coating work and the relationship between material specifications and product performance.

The main concern coming out of the conversation is engagement and role fit. Tom stated that he is increasingly interested in moving out of the day-to-day Apex work and into a role with more forward-looking development responsibility. He specifically mentioned Advanced Materials as an area he would like to explore, particularly work involving coatings, tribology, and test-method development.

Tom did not characterize this as an immediate resignation risk, but he was candid that he has felt discouraged and “stuck” since the recall announcement. He described the current work as highly reactive and said he is spending more time revisiting prior decisions than doing engineering he considers productive. He was careful not to raise a specific complaint about any individual. His comments were more generally about the volume of follow-up requests, the pace of cross-functional review, and his concern that technical input is sometimes sought after decisions have already been framed.

I recommend that Tom’s manager schedule a focused retention conversation before the end of August. The discussion should acknowledge his contributions, clarify near-term expectations, and ask directly what type of work would make the next 12–18 months sustainable for him. Given his background, a lateral move or partial assignment to Advanced Materials could be a reasonable option by Q4, subject to business need and headcount planning.

To: Tom Halvorsen, Sr. Design Engineer, Veridian Orthopedics, Inc.
From: Meridian Testing Labs
Subject: ISO 14242 Wear Test Report - ApexHip Prototype Lot P-001

Report No.: MTL-16-4478
Protocol: MTL-WEAR-14242-16 Rev. B
Test Article: ApexHip metal-on-metal total hip prototype assemblies, Lot P-001

1. PURPOSE

At Veridian Orthopedics’ request, Meridian Testing Labs performed wear simulation testing on ApexHip prototype total hip assemblies to evaluate bearing wear under the conditions defined in ISO 14242. Testing was conducted in accordance with the approved protocol, MTL-WEAR-14242-16 Rev. B, dated 18 November 2016.

2. TEST ARTICLES AND SETUP

Five ApexHip prototype assemblies from Lot P-001 were received on 21 November 2016. Each assembly consisted of a cobalt-chromium femoral head and matching cobalt-chromium acetabular cup. The cup specimens included the KinetiCoat porous titanium exterior coating; coating performance was not evaluated as part of this wear test.

Assemblies were mounted in the multi-station hip simulator using a nominal cup inclination angle of 45 degrees. The simulator applied the ISO 14242 gait loading and motion profile in bovine serum lubricant, diluted to the protein concentration specified by the protocol. One loaded control assembly was maintained under soak conditions for correction of fluid uptake.

Testing was run to five million cycles, with gravimetric measurements obtained at one-million-cycle intervals. Component surfaces were visually inspected at each interval for gross damage, discoloration, or abnormal wear patterning.

3. RESULTS

The mean calculated volumetric wear rate for the four test assemblies was 2.1 mm3 per million cycles. Individual specimen results ranged from 1.8 to 2.4 mm3 per million cycles. No specimen demonstrated a progressive increase in wear rate over the test duration.

| Measurement | ApexHip Prototype Lot P-001 | ClassicHip Predicate Reference* |
|---|---:|---:|
| Mean volumetric wear rate | 2.1 mm3/million cycles | 5.8 mm3/million cycles |
| Range | 1.8–2.4 mm3/million cycles | 4.9–6.7 mm3/million cycles |
| Test duration | 5 million cycles | 5 million cycles |

*Predicate reference values supplied by Veridian from its ClassicHip wear-performance file.

Visual inspection identified light, uniform polishing of the bearing surfaces consistent with simulator operation. There was no gross scratching, deformation, fracture, or evidence of abnormal material loss observed under the tested conditions.

4. SCOPE LIMITATIONS

All testing was conducted at the standard 45-degree cup inclination angle specified in the approved protocol. No testing was performed at elevated or reduced inclination angles, under edge-loading conditions, or under deliberately malpositioned assembly conditions. Accordingly, this report does not characterize wear performance outside the tested 45-degree configuration.

5. CONCLUSION

ApexHip prototype units from Lot P-001 demonstrated a mean wear rate of 2.1 mm3 per million cycles during ISO 14242 simulation testing. This result is within the wear-performance target provided by Veridian and compares favorably with the ClassicHip predicate reference values. Based on the testing performed, the ApexHip design meets wear performance targets under the tested conditions.

CHANGE CONTROL BOARD — MEETING MINUTES

Meeting: ECO-2019-118 Review (ApexHip Acetabular Cup Rim Geometry)
Date: April 2, 2019
Time: 10:00–11:15 AM
Location: Warsaw HQ, Building 2, Engineering Conference Room
Recorded by: Tom Halvorsen

Attendees: Tom Halvorsen (Sr. Design Engineer), Priya Raman (Director, Quality & Complaint Handling), Carlos Mendes (Product Manager, ApexHip), Devon Mitchell (Sr. Regulatory Specialist), Dana Okonkwo (VP Regulatory Affairs)

1. Background
Halvorsen presented the February 2019 wear-test re-analysis showing 4–6x increased wear rates at 55-degree cup inclination compared to the 45-degree standard used in the original ISO 14242 protocol (DR-3, Nov 2016). ECO-2019-118 was opened to evaluate a proposed rim geometry modification intended to reduce edge-loading wear at higher inclination angles.

2. Discussion
Halvorsen summarized the Meridian Labs data supporting the wear increase and noted the change would require re-tooling of the cup mold and a new round of bench testing, estimated at 4–6 months and roughly $650K in NRE. Mitchell raised the question of whether the change would trigger a new 510(k) versus a letter-to-file determination; Okonkwo stated that a geometry change of this nature would likely require a new submission given potential impact on predicate equivalence, adding regulatory timeline risk.

Raman reported that current TrackWise complaint volume for metal-ion-related issues remained low (single-digit cluster from the 2018 Atlanta group, TW-2018-0912 et seq.) and that no clear registry signal had yet emerged domestically. Mendes noted commercial concerns about disrupting the "Active Life" launch momentum and asked whether the wear data reflected real-world inclination angles or worst-case bench conditions only. Halvorsen acknowledged the bench testing used a fixed 55-degree angle chosen to stress-test edge loading and that clinical inclination distribution data was not yet available.

The group discussed cost, regulatory burden, and the absence of a confirmed clinical signal at this time as factors weighing against an immediate design change.

3. Resolution
The Change Control Board voted to DEFER ECO-2019-118. The board found insufficient clinical signal and complaint trend evidence at this time to justify the cost and regulatory risk of the proposed rim geometry change. The board will revisit the decision upon receipt of additional wear data and updated complaint trending.

Vote: 4 in favor of deferral (Raman, Mendes, Mitchell, Okonkwo), 1 opposed (Halvorsen), recommending continued monitoring.

4. Action Items
- Raman to compile a quarterly complaint trend summary for ApexHip metal-ion/wear-related events, due end of Q2 2019.
- Halvorsen to continue informal wear testing at varied inclination angles outside formal ECO scope, results to be shared at next review.
- Mitchell to note deferral rationale in the DHF change log for ECO-2019-118.
- Next review to be scheduled upon receipt of updated data, no later than Q4 2019.

Minutes approved by consensus of attendees present.
